interviewQuestions.question: Design a stack that supports push, pop, top, and retrieving the minimum element, all in O(1).
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The naive idea — scan the stack for the minimum whenever `get_min()` is called — is O(n) per call, so the design has to track the minimum incrementally instead of recomputing it.

My approach: each stack entry stores a pair, `(value, min_so_far)`, where `min_so_far` is the minimum of everything in the stack up to and including that entry at the time it was pushed. On push, I compute the new minimum as `min(new_value, current_top's min_so_far)` and store it alongside the value. `get_min()` just reads the top entry's second field — O(1), no scanning. Pop simply removes the top entry, and the entry now exposed at the top already carries the correct minimum for that earlier state, because it was computed and frozen at push time.

The key insight that makes this work: popping doesn't need to *recompute* anything, because the previous minimum was already saved, not derived. That's the general pattern for adding an O(1) query to a stack — carry a small snapshot of the answer alongside each entry rather than trying to reconstruct it from what remains.

I'd also mention the alternative — a separate auxiliary min-stack that only pushes when the minimum actually changes — as a more memory-efficient variant, at the cost of an extra structure to keep synchronized correctly on every pop.

**Testing:** whether you can extend a structure with a new O(1) guarantee without accidentally introducing an O(n) cost somewhere.

interviewQuestions.question: How do you correctly distinguish a full circular queue from an empty one, and why is this genuinely ambiguous with a naive implementation?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
A circular queue tracked with only a `front` and `rear` index runs into a real ambiguity: filling the buffer completely causes `rear` to wrap around and land exactly on `front` — the identical index relationship an empty queue also has. Front-equals-rear alone can't tell you which state you're in.

Three standard fixes, and I'd pick based on the constraints given: keep an explicit `size` counter alongside front and rear — simplest, and what I'd default to, since checking `size == 0` or `size == capacity` is unambiguous regardless of index positions. Alternatively, deliberately waste one slot in the buffer so the queue is considered full when there's exactly one empty slot left, making full and empty produce genuinely different index states without extra memory for a counter. Or, keep a boolean flag set specifically on the enqueue call that causes a wraparound collision, cleared on the next dequeue.

I'd lead with the size-counter version unless memory-per-element is under real pressure — it's the least error-prone to implement and reason about, and the extra integer is negligible next to a whole buffer slot.

The broader lesson: whenever a structure's state is represented only by index positions instead of an explicit count, check whether two different real situations can collapse to the same index pattern — that's exactly what happened here.

**Testing:** whether you can spot a representation ambiguity before it becomes a debugging session.

interviewQuestions.question: Design a stack that supports push, pop, and "increment the bottom k elements by val" — all better than O(k) per increment call in the amortized sense.
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
Applying the increment immediately, by walking down and adding `val` to each of the bottom k elements, is the obvious approach but costs O(k) per call — fine occasionally, expensive if increments happen often relative to pops.

The better design defers the work with a lazy-propagation trick: keep a separate array, `pending`, the same size as the stack. When an increment call targets the bottom k elements, instead of touching them, record `pending[k - 1] += val` — meaning "whatever eventually gets popped from index ≤ k-1 should include this pending amount." On an actual pop, I apply `pending[top_index]` to the value being returned, then push that same pending amount down one level — `pending[top_index - 1] += pending[top_index]` — before clearing it at the current level, so the deferred increment still correctly reaches whatever gets exposed next.

This spreads the O(k) worst-case cost of one increment call across up to k future pop calls instead of paying it all at once — each individual pop does O(1) extra work, and the total extra work across all pops is bounded by the total amount ever recorded in `pending`, giving an amortized O(1) per operation overall.

I'd flag one interaction worth naming if asked to also support get-minimum on this stack: a batched increment changes values outside the normal push path, so any minimum cached the min-stack way needs explicit handling or it can go stale.

**Testing:** whether you can invent a lazy/deferred-update scheme rather than defaulting to eager recomputation.
